title: Comparing civilizations without erasing uncertainty
summary: Calling a civilization powerful or declining does not yet explain what is happening. Territory, population, knowledge, institutions and external connections can move in different directions. The Atlas separates these questions to describe a historical structure, not to calculate a civilization's overall score.

blocks.text: Calling a civilization powerful or declining does not yet explain what is happening. Territory, population, knowledge, institutions and external connections can move in different directions. The Atlas separates these questions to describe a historical structure, not to calculate a civilization's overall score.

Scale, density, capacity and load require separate attention. Denser exchange can support specialization while increasing dependence. Larger organizations can mobilize resources while bearing the costs of governing greater distances. An advantage in one dimension does not automatically cancel a difficulty in another.

A trajectory connects several moments. A society may contract politically while its religion or knowledge spreads. Comparing civilizations therefore requires an explicit unit, period and dimension. Different capabilities at different stages cannot responsibly be compressed into one ranking.

Coordinates are themselves a limited form of compression, not a promise of exact measurement. Where evidence is incomplete, interpretation contested or reconstruction necessary, uncertainty must remain visible. Identifying what cannot be established does not end inquiry. It allows later evidence to revise the present account.
